title: Standard reference frame for this catalogue
coverage: Names, institutions, and dates on which the usual handbooks agree and for which this pass did not reopen a statute or chronicle
notes: Default frame. A row that cites only GENERAL has not been checked against a specialist edition for this catalogue.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War 1.96
coverage: Aristides' assessment of the Delian League at 460 talents
notes: The initial tribute assessment. Later tribute lists changed the sums. The Greek was not re-transcribed for this catalogue.

title: History of the Peloponnesian War 3.19
coverage: Eisphora of 200 talents in 428 BC
notes: One wartime levy. Not a standing rate.

title: Ab urbe condita 7.16
coverage: Lex Manlia of 357 BC on the vicesima of manumissions
notes: Opened 2026-11-16 in the Grenoble Roman-law transcription of Livy 7.16. The senate approved the tax because the treasury was poor. The vote was taken in the camp at Sutrium.

title: In Verrem on the lex Hieronica
coverage: Sicilian grain tithe of one tenth as Rome administered it
notes: The tithe is the standard content of the lex Hieronica in the Verrines. This pass did not re-read the Latin. Rome kept the system after Sicily became a province in 241 BC.

title: Roman History 55.25
coverage: Five percent inheritance tax established under Augustus
notes: Used through Jane Gardner's discussion and the commentary on Dio 55.25. Dio dates the tax to AD 5; the usual legal date of the lex is AD 6. Dio includes an exemption for the poor that Pliny later assigns to Trajan.

title: Panegyricus 37-40
coverage: Inheritance-tax exemptions for close kin and for small estates
notes: Pliny treats the small-estate exemption as Trajan's. Not reconciled here with Dio.

title: Annals 1.78 and 2.42
coverage: One percent auction tax and its reduction to one half of one percent
notes: Smith's Dictionary, opened 2026-11-16, quotes Tacitus. The tax funded the military treasury. Tiberius halved it after Cappadocia became a province. Dio's account of who raised or cut the rate disagrees; this catalogue follows Tacitus.

title: Life of Caligula 16
coverage: Remission of the auction tax in Italy
notes: Suetonius calls the remitted tax the ducentesima. Coins mark the remission. Whether it stayed abolished is disputed.

title: Life of Caligula 40-41
coverage: Caligula's taxes on food lawsuits porters and prostitutes
notes: Rolfe translation opened 2026-11-16. The food duty is a fixed charge with no sum. The lawsuit rate is one fortieth. The porter rate is one eighth of the daily wage. The prostitute duty is one act's earnings.

title: Life of Vespasian 23
coverage: Tax on urine and the exchange with Titus
notes: Suetonius and Dio 66.14 give the anecdote and no rate. The phrase pecunia non olet is later than these two texts. The year within the reign 69-79 is not given.

title: Annals 13.31
coverage: Nero's remission of the four percent tax on slave sales
notes: The tax's name vicesima quinta is itself one twentieth-fifth that is 4 percent. This catalogue uses the remission in AD 57 as the dated evidence and does not fix the year the tax began. A Gallo-Roman handbook restates the same 4 percent: https://www.persee.fr/doc/gaciv_1251-5612_1993_dic_1_1_859_t1_0123_0000_3

title: Jewish War 7.218
coverage: Two drachmas a head paid to the Capitol
notes: Josephus says Vespasian laid this on Jews wherever they were. Egyptian receipts show women and children paying. Those receipts are not European but the literary rule is empire-wide. Suetonius Domitian 12 describes harsh collection. Nerva's coins advertise a reform of the abuse not the end of the tax.

title: Administration et fiscalité douanières sous le règne d'Auguste
publisher_or_project: Mélanges de l'École française de Rome
coverage: Date and 2.5 percent rate of the Quadragesima Galliarum
notes: The rate is the name of the tax one fortieth. France argues for a creation under Augustus between 20 and 10 BC and favours the stay of 16-13 BC. De Laet had preferred Tiberius. The row uses c. 15 BC as that argument not as an inscribed day.

title: Capitulare Haristalense
author_or_editor: Charlemagne and the assembly at Herstal
coverage: Frankish tithe made obligatory
notes: The MGH text is the edition linked from the standard account of the March 779 capitulary. Article 7 is the usual locus of the universal tithe. This pass used the edition's existence and the standard chapter count not a fresh Latin collation.

title: Kommerkion glossary entry
coverage: Ten percent customs duty called dekate
notes: The entry says the kommerkion appears in the sources about 800 and was 10 percent of the merchandise. Italian privileges later cut or removed it for named cities. The 1082 chrysobull's date is debated and is not used as a second rate.

title: Ordinance of the Saladin Tithe
publisher_or_project: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook transcription of Cave and Coulson
coverage: Ten percent of rents and movables
notes: English ordinance of 1188. Knights' arms horses and clothing clergy books vestments and church goods and precious stones were excluded. Crusaders were exempt. Philip II announced the same tenth in France and then drew back.

title: Magna Carta 1215 clauses 2 12 and 15
publisher_or_project: Magna Carta Project University of East Anglia
coverage: Reliefs and the limit on feudal aids
notes: Clause 2 fixes the old relief at 100 pounds for an earl's barony 100 pounds for a barony and at most 100 shillings for a knight's fee. Clause 3: an heir who comes of age after a minority pays no relief. Aids are limited to ransom knighting the eldest son and one marriage of the eldest daughter and must be reasonable. No sum is fixed for the aid.

title: Christian Córdoba chapter 3
coverage: Castilian alcabala at 5 percent in 1342 and a nominal 10 percent under the Catholic Monarchs
notes: Also cites the local origin as a Muslim municipal due. Edwards notes that under Philip II some villages still paid about 3.5 percent. Ladero Quesada Anuario de Estudios Medievales 22 1992 describes the rate rising through about 3.3 and 5 percent toward 10.

title: gabelle
coverage: Salt tax of pre-revolutionary France
notes: Britannica: in the 14th century gabelle could mean any sales tax; an ordinance of 1360 made it permanent; in the 15th century the name narrowed to salt. Abolished in March 1790. A Wikipedia account also dates a royal salt tax to 16 March 1341. This catalogue does not pick one foundation day.

title: Compte rendu au roi
coverage: Provincial salt prices in the grandes gabelles
notes: The opened page prints Isle-de-France at 60 livres 7 sous and other generalities between about 54 and 62 livres. A later extract of the same report calls the average about 62 livres per quintal or minot. This catalogue does not turn that price into a percent of the marsh price.

title: Tenth Penny
coverage: Alba's proposed 10 percent sales tax
notes: Announced March 1569 not to start until 1571. The hundredth penny was 1 percent once on property. The twentieth penny was 5 percent on transfers of real estate. The tenth was 10 percent on other sales each time the goods were sold. The States accepted the hundredth penny. The tenth was not established as a lasting tax.

title: Fire-Hearth and Stoves Act 1662
coverage: Two shillings a year for every hearth or stove
notes: Royal assent 19 May 1662. Charge begins 25 March 1662 in the act's words and the first payment is Michaelmas 1662. Paid in two equal parts at Michaelmas and Lady Day. Abolished in 1689. Exemptions for the poor were widened after the original act; the poor-relief tests are not copied from the sections opened here.

title: Window tax
author_or_editor: English Wikipedia and the Lincoln Institute summary of the 1696 schedule
publisher_or_project: Wikimedia / Lincoln Institute of Land Policy
coverage: 1696 house and window schedule
notes: Introduced in England and Wales under William III by 7 and 8 Will. 3 c. 18. Flat 2 shillings per house plus 4 shillings if there were 10 to 20 windows plus 8 shillings if there were more than 20. Those totals match the Oxford Companion's bands of 2 6 and 10 shillings. Scotland from 1748. Repealed 1851. The schedule was rewritten many times after 1696.

title: Land Tax Act 1692 4 Will. and Mar. c. 1
publisher_or_project: legislation.gov.uk text from British History Online
coverage: Four shillings in the pound on annual land value for one year
notes: The act also charges 24 shillings on every 100 pounds of personal estate and 4 shillings in the pound on office salaries with soldiers and sailors on muster excepted. First quarterly payment 25 March 1693. The grant was for one year for the war with France. Later annual acts turned the land charge into a county quota. Four shillings was then the wartime rate not a new survey.

title: French poll tax of 1695 and the tariff in a transcription of the declaration
author_or_editor: English Wikipedia / Wikisource transcription of the 1695 classes
coverage: Twenty-two classes from 2000 livres to 1 livre
notes: Declaration at Versailles 18 January 1695. Class followed rank not a measured income. The clergy compounded: the Wikipedia account says 4 million livres a year then 10 million for 1695 and 1696. One popular summary puts the last class at 20 livres; the tariff transcription used here says 1 livre. People tallied below 40 sous were exempt.

title: Vingtième
coverage: Five percent of income from 1749 and the 1710 dixième
notes: Machault d'Arnouville. Registered 19 May 1749. One twentieth of revenue from land offices and industry. A second vingtième in 1756 and a third in 1760. The clergy's land was released in 1751. The same articles describe Louis XIV's dixième of 1710 as a wartime tenth of income. The edict text was not reopened.

title: Is it possible to make money from beards?
coverage: Beard decree of 16 January 1705 and its tariff
notes: Quotes the Complete Collection of the Laws no. 2015. Courtiers servicemen and clerks 60 roubles a year; gosti of the first rank 100; middling merchants and townsmen 60; a third rank including coachmen and Moscow residents 30; priests and deacons exempt; peasants 2 dengi that is 1 kopeck each time they passed a town gate. The State Historical Museum token label agrees. Average yield 1705-1708 was only a few thousand roubles.

title: E179 document notes on the 1380 grant
coverage: Poll tax granted at Northampton in November 1380
notes: Lay persons over 15 except beggars. The vill was to pay 12 pence a head. Neighbours were to help the poor. Nobody was to pay more than 60 groats for himself and his wife nor less than one groat 4 pence for himself and his wife. Collected in 1381. A second collection after widespread under-return was the immediate spark of the rising.

title: The three poll taxes 1377-1381
author_or_editor: Carolyn Fenwick's subject as reviewed in The Medieval Review and the English Wikipedia summary
coverage: Flat 4 pence in 1377 and a graduated tax in 1379
notes: The 1377 grant was a flat 4 pence on each lay person aged 14 or older who was not a beggar. The 1379 grant was graduated by rank for lay people aged 16 or older. The class sums of 1379 are not copied in this catalogue. Parliament granted them for the French war while Richard II was a minor.

title: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle on the payments called Danegeld
coverage: Lump payments to Viking armies from 991
notes: The chronicle records successive lump sums. They are not a rate per hide and are not converted here. The later English geld was a separate hidage tax whose shilling rate was set by each writ.

title: Sound Dues
coverage: Toll at Helsingør from 1429
notes: Eric of Pomerania is the king associated with the 1429 due. The original charge is usually given as one noble per ship. Later treaties replaced that with tariffs. Abolished in 1857. No single percent is entered because the tariff changed.

title: Droit annuel or paulette
coverage: Annual sixtieth on venal office from 1604
notes: The December 1604 edict under Henry IV let an office-holder hand the office on if he paid one sixtieth of its value each year. The financier Paulet administered it. The edict text was not reopened for this row.

title: Ship money writs and the 1641 abolition
coverage: Writs from 1634 extended inland in 1635 and condemned by statute in 1641
notes: Assessed sums on communities. Not a percent of income. Levied by Charles I in Council without a parliamentary grant. Hampden's case contested it. The act of 1641 declared the levy illegal.

title: Excise ordinance of 1643
coverage: Duties on ale and beer
notes: The ordinance introduced a domestic excise collected by parliamentary commissioners. The pence per barrel are not transcribed here. Later excises on soap candles leather and other goods belong to this family and are not given separate rows unless a rate was opened.

title: Brick duty and hat duty of 1784
coverage: Excises of 1784 on bricks and on hats
notes: Both are statutes of George III's Parliament in 1784. The brick duty was charged per thousand bricks and encouraged larger bricks. The hat duty required a stamp. The pence schedules were not transcribed. Both repeals fall after 1788 and are not treated as part of the early-modern rate.

title: Ordonnance associated with the Estates of Orléans
coverage: Royal taille as an annual direct tax
notes: From 1439 the king collected the taille without asking the estates each year in the pays d'élection. It was a sum repartitioned across parishes not a percent of income. Nobles performing military service and the clergy were largely outside the taille personnelle of the north. The south taxed land taille réelle. No kingdom-wide percent exists.

title: Scutage
coverage: Money in place of knight service
notes: A sum per knight's fee set for a campaign. The 1159 Toulouse scutage of Henry II is the usual early royal example. Later rates of one mark two marks or three marks occur in the pipe rolls and are not reduced here to one rate or to a percent of income.

title: Manorial incidents
coverage: Heriot merchet champart and mill banality
notes: These are customs written into custumals and charters. Heriot is the best beast. Merchet is a marriage fine. Champart is a share of the crop fixed locally. A mill banality forces use of the lord's mill for a share of the grain. No European percent is entered.

title: Annates
coverage: One year's revenue of a benefice
notes: By John XXII's pontificate the first year's revenue of many new benefices was owed to the papal camera. The charge is once not an annual percent. The constitution was not reopened.

title: Clerical tenth
coverage: Ten percent of clerical income when a tenth was granted
notes: A tenth was 10 percent for a stated term. Popes granted them for crusades and kings often took the proceeds. It was not a tax that ran every year by its own name.

title: Purveyance
coverage: Compulsory purchase for the household and the army
notes: The right was to take goods and pay for them. The grievance recorded in petitions is payment below the market or long in arrears. Statutes repeatedly limited it. There is no percent.

title: Tallages on the English Jewry
coverage: Arbitrary communal tallages ending with the expulsion of 1290
notes: Henry III and Edward I set the sums by order. They are not a stable percent. The Statute of the Jewry is 1275. The expulsion is 1290. No one pound total is entered.

title: Millones
coverage: Excise on six staples granted in 1590
notes: Philip II's government received a multi-year grant of duties on wine vinegar oil meat soap and candles. The duties were sums per unit. They were renewed and increased. No one percent is entered.

title: Lex Papia Poppaea
coverage: Inheritance disabilities of the unmarried and the childless
notes: AD 9. This is the text people call a bachelor tax. It limited the inheritances and legacies an unmarried or childless citizen could take. It is not a percent paid into the treasury on a tariff. The earlier lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus belongs to the same policy.

title: Collatio lustralis or chrysargyron
accessed: Trade tax collected every five years and abolished in 498
column10: Constantine is credited with the levy on traders and craftsmen payable in gold and silver every five years. Anastasius abolished it in 498. No percent survives in the sources used here. Later narratives stress that very small traders were caught.

title: Fifteenth and tenth
coverage: Lay subsidy frozen as a quota in 1334
notes: The name is one fifteenth of movable goods in the countryside and one tenth in the towns and on ancient demesne. From 1334 a grant was a multiple of the quota then fixed rather than a new valuation of everyone's goods. Earlier fractional subsidies existed. The pound yield of the quota is not entered.
